meaning: Devotion, loving attachment, faith — worship and piety directed toward the divine, esp. as a religious principle and means of salvation.

phonemes.desc: The bh is a voiced aspirate — “b” with breath; not a plain English b.
Short a as in “cup”; the root is bhaj, “to share, partake, adore”.
The abstract ending: “devotion”, “participation” — the quality made a noun.

kin.label: Root

pronunciation.note: The word begins as “partaking” — devotion as sharing in the divine, not mere adoration.

domains.title: Devotion, Loving Attachment to the Divine
domains.subtitle: The Path of Loving Participation
domains.lead: Bhakti is devotion as a complete path: the loving attachment to a personal god that the Bhagavadgītā crowns as the easiest and swiftest way, and that the medieval saints of Tamil country made into India’s most popular religion. From temple hymns sung in the vernacular to the quiet love of the quietist traditions, bhakti is the subcontinent’s answer to the question: how shall an ordinary person love the infinite?

cards.name: The Path of Love
cards.desc: The Bhagavadgītā’s ninth teaching: “offer me even a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water — I accept it”.

cards.name: The Āḻvārs
cards.desc: The twelve Tamil poet-saints whose hymns to Viṣṇu founded the tradition — composed, not compiled.

cards.name: Nāma-Saṅkīrtana
cards.desc: The chanting of the name — Hare Krishna, Rāma Rāma — as devotion’s simplest engine.

cards.name: Grace over Works
cards.desc: Prapatti, śaraṇāgati — the “surrender” that asks nothing and receives everything.

mythology.lead: Bhakti has no biography — it is the biography of millions. Its ‘myths’ are the movement’s own history: the Gītā’s canonization of devotion, the Tamil saints’ songs, the Maharashtrian kīrtan, and the global chant of the Hare Krishna movement. The tradition’s foundational stories cluster around the saints themselves — the hagiographies of Mirabai, Tukaram, and the gopīs of Braj.

myths.title: The Easiest Path
myths.text: Krishna’s ninth discourse tells the anxious that devotion needs no learning, no wealth, no austerity: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water — given with love, accepted. The verse is the charter of every subsequent bhakti movement, and the most quoted single sentence of the Gītā in the modern world.

myths.title: The Poet-Saints of Tamil Country
myths.text: Between the sixth and ninth centuries, twelve poet-saints — Nammāḻvār foremost — sang Viṣṇu into Tamil verse, walking the temple towns and composing the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham, four thousand hymns still sung daily. The bhakti they invented was personal, vernacular, and ecstatic — religion in the mother-tongue, against the Sanskrit monopoly.

myths.title: The Love of the Gopīs
myths.text: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa’s tenth book tells of the cowherd women who loved Krishna past shame, past reason — their love the tradition’s highest image of devotion: uncalculating, unrequited-looking, and finally rewarded. The rasa-theologians read it as the soul’s love for god; the devotees simply wept.

myths.title: The Chant Goes Global
myths.text: From Caitanya’s sixteenth-century Bengali kīrtans to the Hare Krishna movement’s twentieth-century global sankīrtana, the name-chant carried bhakti around the world. The mahāmantra — sixteen words, one call — became the most widely sung Sanskrit formula on earth.

lore.syncretism: Bhakti absorbed the whole pantheon: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Devī, and the unnameable all received the same love. It crossed into Sufism — the bhakti-sant poets read like Rūmī’s cousins — and into Christianity via the Syrian churches of the Malabar coast. The modern global movements (ISKCON, Sathya Sai) are bhakti’s export form.
lore.culturalLegacy: The bhakti movement rewrote Indian religion in the vernaculars — its hymns are the founding literature of half a dozen languages. ‘Bhakti’ entered English as a loan-word in the nineteenth century; and the Hare Krishna chant remains, measured by human-hours, the most performed Sanskrit text in history.
lore.extendedMeditation: Bhakti: the shortest word for the largest love. Restored plainly, it needs no mark — the aspiration of the bh is the only ornament devotion ever wanted, and English “bh” is close enough for love. The lexicon keeps it as the path’s own name for itself.
lore.archaeology: Bhakti’s monuments are the great temple-towns it animated — Śrīraṅgam, Kanchipuram, Pandharpur — and the palm-leaf hymnals of the Prabandham. The modern ISKCON temples of a hundred cities are its newest layer.
lore.cult: Its liturgy is song: the nāma-saṅkīrtana of the name, sung in streets and kitchens. The ārādhana worship of the big temples is bhakti’s formal rite — the god fed, bathed, and sung to sleep like a beloved guest.
lore.iconography: The flute and the cowherd (Krishna-bhakti), the liṅga and the river (Śiva-bhakti), the goddess of the pandals (Devī-bhakti) — bhakti has no single icon because it has no single beloved. Its emblem is the joined palms: the gesture itself.
lore.reception: Religious studies uses bhakti as the type-case of devotional religion: emotional, vernacular, anti-elitist, and unstoppably popular. The movement’s historians (A. K. Ramanujan foremost) made the bhakti poets canonical world literature; and the Hare Krishna chant made the word familiar in every airport on earth.
